The Diving

Ten dives across East Bali's best sites, plus an optional night dive

Wreck, walls, drop-offs, and pelagics, guided by Gusty, a local dive master who's spent his life in these waters.

Liberty Wreck

A 120m WWII cargo ship sitting just off the beach in Tulamben, the most-dived wreck in the world for good reason. Shore entry over volcanic rock, resident bumphead parrotfish, a school of jacks, and coral covering every surface.

Shore DiveWreckMax ~30m / 100ftCurrent: Calm

Coral Garden

Right next to the Liberty, a shallow, richly grown reef of hard and soft coral. This is the macro-photography dive: nudibranchs, pygmy seahorses, the small stuff Tulamben is known for.

Shore DiveReef / MacroMax ~15mCurrent: Calm

The Drop-Off

A wall that starts in a couple of meters of water and falls away fast, formed from lava after Mount Agung's 1963 eruption. Reef sharks and turtles patrol it regularly.

Shore DiveWallMax ~30mCurrent: Calm–Mild

Jemeluk Wall

A rich coral wall along Amed's Jemeluk Bay. Gray reef, white-tip, and black-tip sharks all show up here, alongside dense, healthy coral cover.

Shore DiveWallMax ~25mCurrent: Mild–Moderate

Amed Pyramids

An artificial reef of sunken pyramid structures, now colonized by coral and stacked with reef life: snapper, pufferfish, ghost pipefish, blue-spotted stingrays, and garden eels on the sandy stretches between.

Boat DiveArtificial ReefMax ~20mCurrent: Mild

Gili Biaha

Known for its shark cave, where white-tip reef sharks rest during the day in a sheltered lagoon. A shallower, calmer dive than some of the boat sites, but the sharks are close to guaranteed.

Boat DiveShark CaveMax ~20mCurrent: Moderate

Manta Point

The dive everyone books this trip for. A shallow cleaning station off Nusa Penida with a manta encounter rate around 95%. Conditions can bring surge and current, but this is the payoff dive.

Boat DiveDrift / Cleaning StationMax ~15mCurrent: Moderate

Reefs Along the Way

Beyond the named sites, East Bali is lined with healthy fringing reef, soft corals, reef fish, and the everyday life that fills the water between the headline dives.

Boat / Shore DiveReefMax ~18mCurrent: Mild

Night Dive

An optional add-on for anyone who wants it: back on the Liberty after dark, when the giant bumphead parrotfish tuck in for the night and a different cast of nocturnal creatures comes out to work the same reef.

Shore DiveWreck / MacroMax ~18mCurrent: CalmOptional

Water stays 81–83°F year-round, so a 3mm wetsuit is plenty. Open Water certification is the minimum for the whole trip; Manta Point runs smoother with Advanced Open Water or deeper current experience. Flag it at booking if you're unsure and we'll help you decide.

Not every dive is listed here. The remaining sites on your 10-dive itinerary are chosen by Gusty, your local dive guide, based on conditions, tides, and what's running best that week.

Know Before You Land

A little bit about Bali

Where
An island province of Indonesia, between Java and Lombok. You'll be based in Candidasa, on the quieter east coast.
Language
Indonesian is official; Balinese is the everyday local language. English is widely spoken in tourist areas and dive operations.
Currency
Indonesian Rupiah (IDR). Cards are common in resorts; cash is king for small shops and warungs.
Time Zone
WITA (UTC+8), no daylight saving.
Religion
Predominantly Balinese Hindu, the only Hindu-majority province in Muslim-majority Indonesia. Temples, daily offerings, and ceremonies are part of everyday life.
Climate
Tropical, two seasons: dry (roughly April–October) and wet (November–March). Water temps stay warm year-round.
Before You Go

Entry & visa, handled simply

01

Check your passport. Valid at least 6 months beyond your return date.

02

Get your e-VOA before you fly. US citizens need a visa for Indonesia: the Electronic Visa on Arrival (~$35, 30 days, extendable once) lets you skip the airport line. Apply directly through the official government portal: evisa.imigrasi.go.id. That's the only official site; third-party "visa agent" sites often charge inflated fees.

03

File the All-Indonesia Arrival Card and Electronic Customs Declaration online, within 3 days of arrival. Both are free and mandatory.

04

Pay the Bali Tourist Levy (IDR 150,000, about $10) online in advance through the official Love Bali site or app.

05

Get dive accident insurance, not just trip insurance. Regular travel insurance usually doesn't cover decompression sickness, hyperbaric treatment, or dive-specific emergency evacuation. You'll want both:

  • Regular travel insurance — covers trip cancellation, lost luggage, general medical, and non-dive emergencies. A few well-known options to compare: World Nomads, Allianz Travel, and Travelex Insurance. We have no affiliation with any of these — they're just a starting point to compare plans and pricing.
  • Dive accident insurance from DAN (Divers Alert Network) — covers decompression sickness, hyperbaric treatment, and dive-specific emergency evacuation. This is the standard in the dive world, and membership plus a plan runs cheap for what it covers.
06

Non-US passport holders: check with your local Indonesian embassy well in advance, requirements differ by nationality.

Questions

Frequently Asked

Fly into Ngurah Rai International Airport (DPS) in Denpasar, Bali. Airport transfers on arrival and departure are included.

There are no direct flights from Miami to Bali, expect one or two stops and roughly 24 to 30 hours of total travel time. Because Bali runs 12 hours ahead of Miami, you'll typically land two calendar days after you depart, even though you're not actually traveling for two full days. For this trip's start date of Wednesday, August 25, 2027, plan to depart Miami around Monday, August 23, aiming to land in Denpasar (DPS) by early-to-mid afternoon on the 25th so the included airport transfer goes smoothly. Flying from a different city? Use the same math: check your total flight time to Denpasar, then count back using Bali's 12-hour-ahead time difference to land on your target date. This is a planning estimate, not a guaranteed schedule, exact routing varies by airline (common connections run through Doha, Dubai, or Tokyo), so confirm your specific flight's arrival time once you're ready to book.

Yes, US citizens need an Electronic Visa on Arrival (e-VOA) for Indonesia. It's roughly $35, valid 30 days, and you can buy it online ahead of time through the official government portal at evisa.imigrasi.go.id. No need to wait until you land. See "Before You Go" above for the full rundown.

Yes, Open Water certification or higher is required for every guest on this trip. All diving days, including the optional night dive, assume everyone in the water is certified.

Bring your own if you have it, or use ours, tanks, weights, and full rental gear are available for everyone, no extra charge. Most divers bring their own mask and fins for fit and comfort, but nothing is required.

An intimate group, capped at 16 travelers, with a minimum departure of 6. Small enough to stay personal, without feeling like a packaged tour.

Yes, book the double occupancy rate and you'll share a room. Prefer your own space? Book the single occupancy rate instead.

No. Airfare to and from Bali is not included in the land-only price above.
